summary: This proposed standard describes how to represent Label Generation Rulesets (LGRs) in XML. LGRs are rules for validating identifier labels, along with alternate representations of those labels, and are used for example to implement Internationalized Domain Names. A common XML form lets the rules be shared and processed consistently.

plainLanguage.summary: Some rules decide which letters may be used when making a web address in many languages. This gives those rules a standard written form so different programs can read and apply them the same way.

questions: what is a label generation ruleset
subtitle: A standard XML format for the rules that decide which characters and variants a domain registry accepts.

tldr.problem: Registries of internationalized domain names have published their character rules as loosely formatted text or HTML, and the evaluation logic was implicit. Such tables were hard to implement consistently or compare.
tldr.mechanism: A Label Generation Ruleset (LGR) is an XML document with optional metadata, a required list of permitted code points and their variants, and optional rules and actions. Together these assign each label a disposition such as valid, blocked or allocatable.
tldr.outcome: Policies about permitted code points and variants become machine readable and unambiguous, and the RFC defines how to process a label against an LGR. It is not a full registration policy, and it does not cover trademark or fraud rules.

facts.label: Code point notation
facts.value: Uppercase hex, at least 4 digits, no U+ prefix

today: RFC 7940 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2016. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it defines the XML format for LGRs.

sections.title: Why Write Label Rules in XML
sections.content:
A Label Generation Ruleset (LGR) is a set of algorithms that decide whether, and under what conditions, an identifier label is permitted, based on the code points it contains and their context. An LGR holds a list of permissible code points, variant code point mappings and a set of rules that act on them. In Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) deployment these have also been called IDN tables or variant tables.

Administrators of top-level domain registries have historically published their rules as ASCII text or HTML, loosely based on the Language Variant Table format of RFC 3743. RFC 4290 offers a similar model table format. The RFC says experience through the first decade of IDN deployment showed that tables in these formats are difficult to implement and compare consistently. A structured XML format improves machine readability, consistency, reusability and maintainability.

The format is not limited to IDNs. It may also describe ASCII domain name label rulesets or other identifier labels. Other policies, such as those on trademarks or on fraudulent or objectionable words, are normally not covered.
sections.plainLanguage: People used to write the name rules in all sorts of messy ways, so computers read them differently. A single tidy format fixes that.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The format has to be reasonably easy to implement and automatically checkable for mistakes. It must express the valid code points for one administrator's policy, and computed alternatives called variants, which can map one-to-one or many-to-many. Variants can carry explicit dispositions, such as whether to allocate the variant or merely block it, and both variants and code points may depend on context, for example following a certain code point.

Data must be unambiguous so independent implementations get the same results, and policy rules should be explicit rather than hidden in built-in algorithms. LGRs should be easy to compare and merge, and as many existing IDN tables as practicable should migrate to the format. The requirements came from existing published IDN tables and from ICANN's work on an LGR for the DNS root zone.

It is explicitly not a goal to say which code points an administrator should list. Registration policy is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook should be easy for a computer to follow, say clearly what is allowed, and let people compare two rulebooks side by side. It does not say what the rules should be.

sections.title: The LGR Document and Its Metadata
sections.content:
An LGR is a well-formed XML document that conforms to the schema in Appendix D, in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:lgr-1.0. Element names are lowercase and attribute values are matched case-sensitively. A document that is not well-formed or violates the constraints MUST be rejected.

The root lgr element holds up to three sections in this order: an optional meta element, a required data element with the code point data, and an optional rules element with rules and actions.

The metadata is self-documenting and includes version, date (an ISO 8601 full-date), language (a language tag; und-Cyrl for a script-wide Cyrillic LGR), scope (for example the domain to which it applies), description, validity-start and validity-end, unicode-version and references. Apart from unicode-version, software does not need the metadata to compute valid labels or variants. If the LGR depends on Unicode properties, the Unicode version in the form x.y.z MUST be declared, and software without that version's data MUST NOT do whole-label evaluation that relies on those properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook has a cover page saying who wrote it, when and for which language, then the list of allowed letters, then the extra rules. The only cover page detail a computer must check is which version of the Unicode letter book was used.

sections.title: Code Points, Sequences and Variants
sections.content:
The data element lists the repertoire with char elements for single code points or sequences and range elements for inclusive ranges, for example <char cp='002D'/> or <range first-cp='0030' last-cp='0039'/>. Code points are written in uppercase hexadecimal, zero-padded to at least 4 digits and without the U+ prefix. Defining the same code point twice MUST cause the LGR to be rejected.

A char can list a sequence such as 006C 00B7 006C, so the middle dot is only eligible between two letters l. Alternatively a when or not-when attribute names a rule giving the context in which a code point or variant is valid.

Variants are mappings from a code point to other code points, written as var children of a char. A mapping runs in one direction only, so symmetry and transitivity must be spelled out explicitly. A type attribute on a variant describes the resulting disposition. A null variant uses an empty cp, and a reflexive variant maps a code point to itself so its type can trigger actions. Duplicate variant labels are an error.

The ref and comment attributes annotate elements and are ignored in machine processing, while tag attributes group code points into classes.
sections.plainLanguage: You list the allowed letters one by one or in ranges. For look-alike letters you write down which letter can stand in for which, and you must write it both ways yourself.

sections.title: Classes and Rules
sections.content:
The rules element holds character classes and rules. A class is a set of code points defined by a tag in the data, a Unicode property such as property='ccc:9' (the virama), an explicit list, or a combination using complement, union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference. Implementations SHOULD support these Unicode properties: General Category, Script, Canonical Combining Class, Bidi Class, Arabic Joining Type, Indic Syllabic Category and Deprecated. If a program meets an unsupported property it MUST abort with an error.

A rule is a sequence of match operators: any, choice, start, end, char, class, nested rule, and the contextual anchor, look-ahead and look-behind. The count attribute takes forms such as n, n+ and n:m, and matching is greedy like a regular expression. Rules and classes cannot be recursive.

A whole-label rule tests the entire label. A parameterized context rule uses anchor as a placeholder for the code point being checked, with look-behind and look-ahead around it. The RFC shows the Greek lower numeral sign valid only before a Greek-script character, and the rule from RFC 5892 that forbids mixing the two Arabic digit ranges in one label.
sections.plainLanguage: Beyond the plain list, the rulebook can say things like "this mark is only allowed right before that kind of letter" or "you cannot mix these two kinds of digits in one name".

sections.title: Actions and Processing a Label
sections.content:
An action assigns a disp (disposition) to a label when a condition holds. It can use match or not-match with a rule name, or the variant triggers any-variant, all-variants and only-variants. Actions run in file order and the first one triggered decides the label's disposition. The RFC recommends five dispositions: invalid, blocked, allocatable, activated and valid. If no explicit action triggers, default actions apply and end with a catch-all of valid.

To process a label, a consumer first checks that every code point, or the longest matching sequence at each position, is in the repertoire and meets its when and not-when conditions. It then builds variant labels by permuting variant mappings that are valid in context, records the variant types used, and determines each disposition. Variant labels with disposition invalid are removed. Generating a duplicate variant label MUST be treated as an error.

To check whether two labels collide, the RFC points out that variant mappings form disjoint sets. Instead of generating every permutation, it is enough to replace each code point by an index for its set and compare the resulting index labels. The RFC says older formats like RFC 3743 can be expressed in this one, and Appendix B explains the translation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each name gets a verdict, such as fine, blocked or reserved for the same owner. The computer goes through the verdict rules from top to bottom and uses the first one that fits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unrestricted use of non-ASCII characters in security-relevant identifiers such as domain labels can confuse users and invite attacks, because different code points can look identical or mean similar things. An LGR is only a partial remedy. It can prohibit inappropriate code points and group variants so that their labels are mutually exclusive or go to the same owner, and being machine processable it allows automated checks. Conforming to the format does not ensure that an LGR is free of risk, and a case-by-case review of visual confusability is one additional approach.

Implementations also face resource risks. A naive attempt to generate all variant labels can exhaust the machine and cause denial of service, and backtracking in whole-label evaluation can take exponential time on pathological rules or labels. The RFC advises optimization, estimating the number of permutations in advance, and enforcing label length limits.
sections.plainLanguage: A rulebook helps stop confusing look-alike names but cannot stop every trick. A careless program could also get stuck trying every possible spelling, so it should be smart about it.

sections.title: Media Type, Namespace and Disposition Registry
sections.content:
LGRs SHOULD be transmitted with the media type application/lgr+xml, registered by IANA under RFC 6838, with the file extension .lgr and an optional charset parameter as for application/xml in RFC 7303. IANA also registered the namespace URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:lgr-1.0.

The document creates a registry of Label Generation Ruleset Dispositions with two subregistries. Standard Dispositions need Specification Required and start with the five dispositions of Section 7.3. Private Dispositions are first come first served and take the form entity:disposition where the entity is a domain name, for example example.org:reserved. Standard names must not contain a colon and all names are lowercase ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official file label for these rulebooks and an official list of verdict words. Companies can add their own private verdict words by putting their name in front.

items.label: Invalid
items.desc: The resulting string is not a valid label.

items.label: Blocked
items.desc: A valid label that should be blocked from registration.

items.label: Allocatable
items.desc: Reserved for the operator of the origin string but not automatically allocated.

items.label: Activated
items.desc: The string should be activated for use.

items.label: Valid
items.desc: The resulting string is a valid label; the typical default.

viz.caption: MINIMAL LDH LGR FROM APPENDIX A

data.title: Lowercase letters, digits, hyphen
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<lgr xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:lgr-1.0">
<data>
    <char cp="002D" comment="HYPHEN (-)" />
    <range first-cp="0030" last-cp="0039"
      comment="DIGIT ZERO - DIGIT NINE" />
    <range first-cp="0061" last-cp="007A"
      comment="LATIN SMALL LETTER A - LATIN SMALL LETTER Z" />
</data>
</lgr>
